question: Due to their administrative vulnerability, undocumented workers are at a higher risk of being abused by their employers. Directive 2009/52/EC aims to protect workers and sanction abusive employers. Article 13(4) provides for the possibility for Member States to grant residence permits to illegally staying third-country nationals, in order to make it easier for them to lodge complaints against an abusive employer.

In Belgium, it is impossible to prosecute this type of abuse because the Law of 11 February 2013, which provides for sanctions and measures against employers of illegally staying third-country nationals1, has not transposed Article 13(4).

Directive 2011/98/EU (Single Permit Directive), which has been in force in Belgium since 3 January 20192, only applies to legally staying persons and does not allow residence permits to be issued. However, if proceedings of this kind are to be brought against an employer accused of exploitation and violence in the workplace, these residence permits are essential.

Does the Commission believe that Belgium has correctly transposed Directive 2009/52/EC? If so, can it respond to the arguments that have been put forward? If not, does it plan to open an infringement procedure?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.6.2024) Directive 2009/52/EC1 (Employers Sanctions Directive) provides for minimum standards on sanctions and measures against employers of irregularly staying third-country nationals, as well as measures to protect the rights of irregular migrant workers.

The Communication on the application of the Directive 2009/52/EC of 29 October 20212 sets out measures to improve the implementation of this Directive, including on the protection of the rights of irregularly staying migrant workers.

These include training for labour inspectors on the rights of irregularly staying third-country nationals deriving from the Directive, such as back payments, effective complaint mechanisms, and the possibility to grant temporary residence permits in the case of particular criminal offences.

Indeed, Article 13(4) of the Employers Sanctions Directive stipulates that Member States shall define in national law the conditions under which they may grant, on a case-by-case basis, permits of limited duration, linked to the length of the relevant national proceedings, to the third-country nationals involved, in respect of criminal offences under Article 9 (c) or (e), namely when the infringement is accompanied by particularly exploitative working conditions, or when it relates to the illegal employment of a minor.

The Commission is in contact with the Belgian authorities to clarify elements of the transposition of Article 13(4). Lastly, the recast of Directive 2011/98/EU, adopted on 24 April 2024, did not change the scope of the Directive concerning irregular staying third-country nationals.
1 Directive 2009/52/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 June 2009 providing for minimum
standards on sanctions and measures against employers of illegally staying third-country nationals. 2 COM(2021) 592 final.
